analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Davis-Bacon Act, removing prevailing-wage requirements on federally funded construction projects.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the Davis-Bacon wage requirements died in committee without a vote, leaving the prevailing-wage rule for federal construction intact.
analysis.plain_summary: The Davis-Bacon Act requires contractors on federally funded construction projects to pay workers the wage rate that prevails locally for their trade. This bill would repeal that requirement, 30 days after enactment, for new federal construction and repair work. Supporters argued it would save money and cut paperwork; opponents argued it would cut the pay of construction workers on federal projects.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, contractors and subcontractors on federal construction projects would benefit most: they could hire labor at whatever wage the market allows instead of the locally prevailing rate, lowering their labor costs. Some government spending would be freed up, and nonunion crews might find it easier to win federal jobs.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Davis-Bacon Act's requirement that locally prevailing wages be paid to laborers and mechanics on federally financed or assisted construction, alteration, and repair of public buildings and public works.
Also repeals the associated reporting requirements under section 276c of title 40, removing wage-certification paperwork for federal contractors.
For contractors, lower mandated wage floors on federal jobs mean lower bid prices, which supporters argued would reduce federal construction costs.

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federally funded projects would bear the cost. With the prevailing-wage floor gone, contractors could pay below the local standard rate for each trade, and in many areas that would mean lower take-home pay for the skilled tradespeople building public works.

drawbacks.text: The core effect of repeal would be to remove the wage floor that keeps federal construction pay at local trade rates, which would tend to pull down wages for construction workers on public projects.

Prevailing-wage rules are often defended as protecting skilled work quality and limiting a race to the cheapest crew; repeal would rely on market bidding alone to maintain that, with no replacement safeguard included in the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would shift money within federal construction: taxpayers and contractors could save on labor costs, but the savings would come directly out of the paychecks of the workers on those jobs. There is no provision cushioning or offsetting that wage loss, so the trade runs almost entirely from workers to contractors and the federal budget.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee: the House referred it to the Education and Labor Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee, and no action was ever taken before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve King of Iowa introduced the Davis-Bacon Repeal Act in the House on August 3, 2007, with 31 original cosponsors, all Republicans.
A total of 36 representatives cosponsored the bill, all of them Republicans.
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Education and Labor on the day it was introduced.
On September 19, 2007, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and the record shows no further action for the remainder of the 110th Congress.
The bill never received a floor vote, and the Davis-Bacon Act remained in effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction workers who rely on prevailing-wage rules for their pay are better off, since the requirement was never repealed. The federal contractors who would have gained from lower mandated wages got nothing.

industries.note: Repeal would let them pay below the locally prevailing rate on federally funded jobs, cutting labor costs. The saving comes directly out of construction workers' pay, so the industry's gain runs against the workers doing the work.

industries.industry: Construction labor unions and skilled trades
industries.note: Davis-Bacon effectively benchmarks federal construction pay to local trade rates, which union-scale workers benefit from directly. Repeal would remove that floor for workers on federal projects.
Nonunion contractors could more easily win federal bids without certified payroll requirements, but their own crews would lose the prevailing-wage pay floor too.
